Elon Musk says SpaceX plans to start launching its first “StarMind” space computers, co-designed with NVIDIA, around Q3 2027, because adding 200 gigawatts of AI a year on the ground would mean growing the entire US grid 40% annually

“Yeah. So, yes, there’s currently, people have tested NVIDIA GPUs. So there’s a satellite with an NVIDIA GPU up there that we launched, and there’s a satellite we recently launched with a Google TPU, and these are operating, to the best of our knowledge, they’re working fine in space.”

“We expect to start launching the first StarMind computers, which we’ve co-designed with NVIDIA, probably, I’m just guessing here, but in the third quarter of next year. And we’ll start off slow, then it will ramp to significant volume probably in 2028, and then very large volume in 2029.”

“Just as a frame of reference, the average power consumption in the United States is just over 500 gigawatts. So if you look, peak power capability is roughly 1.2 terawatts, but average power consumption is just over 500 gigawatts. So you can really see that. Like if you’re doing, say, 200 gigawatts a year of AI, that would be like doing a 40% increase in the entire US power grid every year, which is simply not feasible.”

items.author: Fred Lambert
items.text:
Tesla just confirmed it will end Cybertruck production in 2027. I think it's one of the best case studies we have on managing customer expectations.

Tesla received more than 1 million reservations for the Cybertruck. Our best estimate puts the real number closer to 2 million. That's demand most automakers can only dream of.

Tesla delivered about 70,000 trucks in three years.

You can point to a lot of factors: the design, the production ramp, quality issues, the brand's politics, competition. They all played a role. But they're small compared to the main one.

Tesla promised a $40,000 truck with up to 500 miles of range. It delivered an $80,000 truck with about 300 miles of range.

Those 1 million+ people didn't reserve the truck Tesla ended up building. They reserved a promise. When the product showed up at twice the price with 40% less range, most of them simply walked away.

items.title: Everyone can win: open-source, frontier labs, infra, apps
items.author: Gavin Baker
items.summary: Baker’s base case is a hybrid multi-model future: open-weight tokens dominate volume, frontier labs still do well, and infrastructure and applications benefit from fragmentation and lower model-layer margins. Lower model margins mechanically raise compute demand so long as someone will pay to train — and he casts Jensen as “trainer of last resort.”

items.title: Fear creates price misallocations — and opportunity
items.author: Chris Camillo
items.summary: Camillo argues young investors will look back and see how fear mispriced strong businesses. Nothing creates greater price misallocations than fear and greed, he writes — and with fear hitting some of the world’s strongest companies, there is little reason to reach for speculative names.

items.title: Who captures the profits of a tech revolution?
items.author: Rose Celine Investments
items.summary: Rose Celine notes that the firms that build revolution-enabling infrastructure are not always the ones that keep most of the eventual profits. Sometimes the biggest winners use that infrastructure to build products or cut costs without carrying the capital burden of building it — a useful lens on AI cloud and memory spend.

items.title: Your dopamine system narrows the search for life-changing choices
items.author: Parmita
items.summary: Parmita argues you always have a million options, but dopamine collapses the search to habits and paths of least resistance. The “hits” that change a life are often no longer than those habits — just inaccessible under the current search conditions until you override the system.

items.title: Four Cards
items.rule: If a person is drinking beer, they must be over 21.
items.explanation: Drinking beer could hide something that breaks the rule; Age 17 breaks it if the other side turns out to be Drinking beer. Age 25 can't break it (the rule never says only those cards have it), and Drinking water isn't covered by the rule at all. Most people pick the card that matches the rule's second half instead of the one that could falsify it. Most people get this version right and the letters-and-numbers version wrong, though the logic is identical.
